transcript.text: Hi, my Hotpoint Aquarius dryer is taking forever to dry and the top gets really hot. Model is TCM580GUK if that helps

From what you have described, the most likely cause is clean the lint filter and the condenser/heat exchanger. Damp laundry is most often an airflow problem, and the first free check is the fluff filter in the door opening — heat-pump models often have a second filter at the bottom too. Was it full of fluff (and is it clean now), is the mesh torn, or was it already clean?
[Safety panel] Clean the lint filter after every load — a build-up of fluff is a fire risk and restricts airflow. Don't run the dryer overnight or while you're out.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the lint filter is" — The fluff/lint filter sits in the door opening or just inside the rim. Lift it out and clear the fluff after every load. Typical layout — your dryer may differ.]

Thank you. The door filter had a thick layer of fluff on it, I'll admit I sometimes forget to clean it. I've also rinsed the condenser unit at the front bottom, which had lint packed on the fins, and it looks much cleaner now. The top of the dryer also gets very hot to the touch, and I often run it while I'm out at work.

Run a normal drying programme with a normal load. Is the laundry coming out dry now, or still damp?
[Safety panel] Clean the lint filter after every load — a build-up of fluff is a fire risk and restricts airflow. Don't run the dryer overnight or while you're out.

I haven't run it again yet, as I've only just finished cleaning the filter and condenser, so I can't say whether it's drying any better. Is there anything else I should check before I put a load through?

Check the vent hose out of the back: it should be short, without kinks or squashed sections, and clear of fluff all the way to the outside vent. Was it kinked, squashed or blocked (and is it sorted), or was it already clear?
[Safety panel] Clean the lint filter after every load — a build-up of fluff is a fire risk and restricts airflow. Don't run the dryer overnight or while you're out.

I'm afraid I'm not sure, as I haven't looked at the back of the dryer. This is a condenser model with a water container, so I wasn't expecting it to have a vent hose at all. Is that something I should be checking on mine?

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. No, a condenser dryer like yours has no vent hose. It condenses the moisture into the water container instead of blowing it outside, so the parts that keep air flowing are the door fluff filter and the condenser unit you've just cleaned. From what you have described, the most likely cause is clean the condenser / heat exchanger (condenser & heat-pump). When did you last clean the lint filter and (on a condenser/heat-pump) the condenser?
[Safety panel] Clean the lint filter after every load — a build-up of fluff is a fire risk and restricts airflow. Don't run the dryer overnight or while you're out.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the condenser and water tank are" — On a condenser dryer the water container pulls out at the top and the condenser/heat exchanger sits behind a flap at the bottom front — slide it out and rinse it. Condenser/heat-pump dryers only; layout may differ.]

I've just cleaned both today, but I'm afraid I can't say when I last did the condenser before that, and the door filter only gets cleaned when I remember. Is there anything else I should check before running a load?

From what you have described, the most likely cause is clean the lint filter and the condenser/heat exchanger. Overloading, or putting clothes in that weren't spun well in the washer, makes drying much slower. The drum should be no more than about two-thirds full. Was it overloaded or were the clothes very wet going in (and have you changed that), or was it a normal, well-spun load?
[Safety panel] Clean the lint filter after every load — a build-up of fluff is a fire risk and restricts airflow. Don't run the dryer overnight or while you're out.
[Helpful to see: image "Tumble dryer not drying properly — what to check" — Poor drying is most often caused by restricted airflow. Clean the fluff filter every cycle, clean the condenser regularly and avoid overloading the drum — these are safe checks you can do yourself. Switch the dryer off and let it cool first.]

It was a normal-sized load from a 1400 spin washer, so I don't think it was overloaded or too wet. The dryer is in a small utility room with the door usually shut, if that matters. Is there anything else I should check?

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. From what you have described, the most likely cause is clean the condenser / heat exchanger (condenser & heat-pump). Run a normal drying programme. Is it collecting the water (and staying dry underneath) now, or still not?
[Safety panel] Clean the lint filter after every load — a build-up of fluff is a fire risk and restricts airflow. Don't run the dryer overnight or while you're out.

I haven't run a new load yet, so I can't say whether it's collecting water any differently. Before the cleaning, the water container was half full and emptied fine. Also, I should mention that the dryer is about 12-14 years old and came with the house, so I don't know if it was ever modified under the Hotpoint fire-safety programme. Should I be worried about that?

It's worth finding out rather than worrying: whether it matters depends on whether your serial number was among the affected machines and, if so, whether it was modified, and you can check on Hotpoint's safety recall checker using the model and serial number from the label. Until you know, only run it while you're home and nearby, not while you're out at work. Run a normal drying programme and stay nearby. Does it run right through now, or still stop part way?
